style.summary:
style of A: A uses brief, minimal responses such as Yeah and an unfinished this is the.
style of B: B speaks in a long, reflective, experience-based style with fillers and self-corrections, sounding relaxed and expert.

A: A's short Yeah responses keep the conversation moving without committing B to a position, so A can steer by staying neutral.
A's unfinished opening this is the frames the topic for B to respond to, which gives A control of the framing.
A's neutrality puts the burden on B to justify the suggestion.
B: B's relaxed, experienced tone gives B authority that A cannot easily contest.
B's self-corrections signal careful thinking that makes B's suggestion seem well considered.
B's reflective register places B in the role of the one who explains and advises.

A: A's neutrality is passive, since B's long turn of experience carries the content that the listener has to accept.
A's framing is only a fragment, so the topic is actually defined by B's explanation that follows.
The burden of justification is a weak lever, because B already has the expertise and can answer without difficulty.
B: B's experience comes from an earlier setting with many features, so A's current needs may make that experience less relevant.
B's self-corrections show uncertainty, which lets A reject the suggestion without needing to refute it.
B's advisory register is only a tone, and A can decide whether the advice applies to the case at hand.

content.summary:
content of A: A offers little substantive content beyond agreeing and introducing the topic.
content of B: B covers substance on visualising many features at once and the value of scatter plots for combined features.

A: A's introduction of the topic defines the subject that the content will address.
A's agreement shapes which of B's points are accepted as relevant.
A's selection of the subject sets the scope of the exchange.
B: B's point that a feature is good alone but may behave differently in combination gives the substance a clear analytic claim.
B's advice to show as many features together sets the method that the content is built on.
B's account of graphics that combine several features supplies concrete examples.

A: A's introduction is brief, and B's analytic claim about combinations is what the content actually concerns.
A's agreement is minimal, so it does not shape which points count as relevant.
A's choice of subject is only a fragment, and B's substance takes over from there.
B: B's analytic claim is a general principle that A can test against the current features, so the substance is open to A.
B's method is a preference from past work and does not bind A's approach.
B's examples are described only vaguely, so A's own judgement determines what is useful.

coordination.summary:
coordination of A: A makes a short turn to start, then yields.
coordination of B: B takes the floor for an extended turn, then trails off with a dash, leaving the next move open.

A: A's short starts give A the first move in each exchange.
A's yielding after a short turn lets A keep control of when the topic changes.
A's quick handoff leaves the sequence in A's hands.
B: B holds the floor for the extended turn, which gives B control over the content.
B's trailing dash leaves the transition in B's hands, so B chooses when to stop.
B's extended explanation sets the order in which ideas are presented.

A: A's first move is only a fragment, so B's extended turn is what determines the direction of the exchange.
A's yielding is compelled by B's floor, so the control of the transition still belongs to B.
A's quick handoff is answered by B's long explanation, so the sequence is effectively B's.
B: B's trailing dash shows the thought is unfinished, so A can take the transition at the point where B stopped.
B's extended turn is interrupted by A's short starts, so the floor is shared.
B's order of ideas is only offered, and A can rearrange them.

engagement.summary:
engagement of A: A is minimally engaged, showing little interest beyond short agreement.
engagement of B: B is engaged, drawing on personal experience with I used to do this a lot.

A: A's minimal involvement lets A stay out of commitments while still shaping the exchange.
A's selective agreement lets A decide which of B's points to take up.
A's lack of enthusiasm forces B to carry the engagement, which gives A leverage.
B: B's personal experience with the topic shows real involvement in the problem.
B's willingness to share past practice makes B the more invested party.
B's account of past use gives B a stake in the outcome that A does not have.

A: A's minimal involvement is a passive stance, and B's engagement is the one that drives the substance.
A's selection of points is limited because B's contribution is extensive, so A's choices matter less.
A's lack of enthusiasm means the leverage is not used, so B's investment carries the discussion.
B: B's experience may not match the current case, so A's neutral position is the more relevant one.
B's stake is in the past work, and A's present decision is what the group actually depends on.
B's investment is shown through anecdote, which A can set aside in favour of the immediate question.
